articles.title: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: Nvidia poured tens of billions into AI startups under Huang. Without him at the helm, founders and VCs are bracing for smaller checks and lower valuations.
articles.full_text:
It was the resignation heard across the world.

Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down . “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.

Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.

Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures.

Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020.

While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.  Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out .

Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street. “She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”  Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.

For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E.

It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs.

Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals.

Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal . “Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world.

The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”  It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly.

By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.

If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.) Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.  Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said.

CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.

While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.

Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said.

The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.

Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations. “When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said.

Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.

Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.

Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”  Topics AI , Jensen Huang , neocloud , nvidia , open source , Startups , Venture When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .

articles.full_text:
AI News Tech ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s Dots agents make purchases for you OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet won’t share your actual credit card info with its AI agents.﻿ OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet won’t share your actual credit card info with its AI agents.﻿ by Stevie Bonifield Nov 13, 2026, 8:45 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech.

Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

After launching its Dots AI agents platform earlier this year, OpenAI is launching a wallet for the agents.

ChatGPT Wallet is rolling out starting today for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US aged 18 and older using a US billing address and “eligible US-issued American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa cards.” After adding a card to the wallet, your Dots agents can use it to buy things in response to your prompts, but they’ll check in with you each time before checking out.

OpenAI’s support page says every purchase with ChatGPT Wallet requires a security check with biometric verification like Face ID or a fingerprint scan.

Image: OpenAI After you review the AI agent’s purchase and sign off on it, OpenAI says that, similar to using tap to pay , Apple Pay , or Google Wallet , it substitutes your credit card details with a payment token, so your actual card info isn’t shared with your Dots agent or the business you’re buying from.

Eventually, OpenAI says it expects “users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases.” ChatGPT Wallet might not work everywhere.

Some retailers have restrictions on AI agents or block them altogether.

Earlier this year, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agents.

OpenAI says that in order for agents to use ChatGPT Wallet, “websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

articles.title: ChatGPT’s new Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out for you
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、AI agent & application
articles.summary: ChatGPT Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out on users' behalf, starting with a limited rollout to U.S. Pro subscribers.
articles.full_text:
ChatGPT can now shop for you.

On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots , help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf.

The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S.

ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express.

OpenAI says that users are fully in control of the purchases, as they’re able to review the items, the total, and the payment card that will be used to complete the transaction before the checkout occurs.

In addition, users will approve the purchases directly with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction.

The addition comes as consumer-facing AI tools are working to find the right product-market fit, in terms of how they can help people be more efficient as they complete various tasks.

While companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity on its app.

Other personal AI agents, like Instinct, also support making purchases on users’ behalf.

It’s no surprise, then, that OpenAI would want to enter this space more with an agentic shopping feature of its own.

To get started, ChatGPT subscribers add their eligible payment cards to the new ChatGPT Wallet, then ask their dot to help with a purchase. (This setup is a one-time thing; users don’t have to re-enter their payment information every time they buy.) When it’s time to transact, ChatGPT’s Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, which is a substitute for the user’s actual card details, so that information isn’t shared with either the dot or the merchant.

The merchant will automatically receive what it needs to fulfill the order from the dot, like the shipping address and contact information, OpenAI says.

The company notes that customers who shop via their dots will still be able to earn their credit card rewards and be able to take advantage of protections that typically come with cards, like being able to dispute transactions.

The limited availability at launch will allow OpenAI to test and improve the feature and its capabilities before rolling it out more broadly.

In the future, the company plans to offer users more control over the feature by allowing them to set spending limits or configure other parameters around purchase categories or time periods, so they can pre-approve purchases that their agent can then handle more autonomously.

It also aims to make the agentic shopping feature an option at a broader number of supported retailers.

This could be a challenge in some areas, where retailers are blocking AI agents from using their site ; on the shopping front, the largest retailer to ban AI agents is Amazon, as it aims to steer users to its own AI agent, Alexa, instead.

To help retailers adapt to agentic commerce, OpenAI also published a Commerce Partner Playbook that offers tools and guidance to sites that want to support customers using agents.

articles.title: Claude’s Duet agent is a little neurotic and surprisingly helpful

articles.summary: Normally, the products I test don't offer to help me write up my experience with them. Duet is different. Claude Duet is Anthropic's AI agent for consumers, the latest attempt by an AI company to try to convince us that agents can be useful for people who don't write code. It's been an interesting couple […]
articles.full_text:
AI Tech Reviews Claude’s Duet agent is a little neurotic and surprisingly helpful Duet is a decent helper, if a little jumpy at times. by Allison Johnson Nov 13, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC Link Share Gift | Photo: Allison Johnson / The Verge Allison Johnson is a senior reviewer with over a decade of experience writing about consumer tech.

She has a special interest in mobile photography and telecom.

Previously, she worked at DPReview.

Normally, the products I test don’t offer to help me write up my experience with them.

Duet is different.

Claude Duet is Anthropic’s AI agent for consumers, the latest attempt by an AI company to try to convince us that agents can be useful for people who don’t write code.

It’s been an interesting couple of months: Instinct gave us an impressive text-based assistant , Meta offered us its cute little guy, Muse, to help us buy things , and OpenAI gave us the more work-oriented Dots .

Claude Duet is even more focused on work than those.

It’s also more consumer-friendly than Claude Cowork , which was more consumer-friendly than Claude Code — the coding agent that kicked off a whole hype cycle earlier this year.

I’ve been testing it over the past week as I navigate a busy travel and work schedule.

At turns it has been truly useful, kind of a nag, and very eager to write about itself.

Duet is still a “research preview” according to Anthropic, and access is limited to Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers in the US, with a waitlist to join.

It’s not here to order you burritos, either; it’s for “professionals and small business owners” and is meant to use its judgment about what needs your attention most.

Related Anthropic takes on Muse with Claude Duet, its new AI agent AI agents are ready to shop.

Some retailers are wary United won’t let your AI agent book your flight Like Meta’s Muse, Duet has its own app. (If you’re keeping score at home, yes, it has been updated to fully support the iPhone Duo).

Duet uses Claude’s characteristically cheery, minimalist design.

The app is consumer-friendly and approachable.

Once you’ve connected all the productivity and chat services you want, it’ll look for ways to help out with and suggest them as cards you can swipe left or right to hide or accept — kind of a to-do list Tinder.

In the name of testing, I went all in on Duet and gave it everything: my work email, calendar, Google Docs, and Slack.

This gave it plenty of grist for the mill in more ways than I’d even realized at first.

Because our biweekly staff meeting is automatically summarized in an email from Gemini, and Duet had access to my email, it was able to connect the dots between something said in a meeting and a direct message in Slack.

Duet also worked out who my boss is because we have a shared Google Doc for our weekly 1:1 meetings.

AI is at its most useful when it can suck up lots of data, and Duet wasted no time doing so.

Previous Next 1 / 2 Duet has started each morning by greeting me with a brief message and some quick highlights for my day, like reminding me to pack an item required for a video shoot before my flight.

Below that, it would suggest to-dos, usually ending in an offer to help draft a message or add an item to an agenda.

This has often been helpful, though it sometimes felt like interacting with a slightly neurotic personal assistant.

In one instance, I’d emailed someone I interviewed for a story that the article was likely to go up on Tuesday and that I’d send a link when it did.

I submitted my draft to my editors late at night on Monday, and Tuesday morning Duet was beside itself.

It wasn’t quite 9AM yet when it pointed out that the story was still waiting for an edit and I needed to get on that — or else I wouldn’t be able to send the link I promised.

The concern was a bit misplaced.

And it didn’t pick up on the nuance in my message implying that this was not a hard deadline, nor the fact that it was only 7AM local time for my editor.

This sometimes felt like interacting with a slightly neurotic personal assistant In other cases, it was surprisingly helpful.

In planning out the next few weeks I’d missed the fact that upcoming time off would only leave me with a couple of working days before another big draft was due.

Duet proposed a solution, offered to update the Google Doc with weekly notes for my editor, and drafted a Slack message for him noting the update.

Reader, the message was a little too good.

It copied my millennial habit of writing in all lowercase — which it pointed out in a slightly self-congratulatory aside — and used an abbreviation we often use to refer to our CMS.

But it also shortened the word “signature” to “sig,” which I never would and made me laugh out loud.

In any case, there’s no fooling anyone; the Slack message was tagged with a “sent with Claude” label.

Duet often volunteered to help start my drafts, which is always a hard no for me.

I’ll type up my own little blogs, thank you very much Claude.

If you’re not a writer, I can see how taking care of little writing chores here and there would be helpful.

But this started feeling like a Spider-Man-pointing-at-Spider-Man moment when the task it wanted to help with was reviewing itself.

Maybe that’s how CEOs live It was a little uncanny, too.

Even setting aside the fact that I was writing about Duet, it’s kind of weird knowing that it can read every email, draft, and Slack I send.

It can read all of that because I opted in to sharing that data , and I knew full well what I was doing.

But it’s another thing to see it in practice.

I wonder if it would change how I work if I knew I didn’t really need to take responsibility for putting things on my calendar, writing down a to-do list, or paying attention in a meeting because Duet will just handle it.

Maybe that’s how CEOs live.

Not that I cherish creating calendar entries, but I wonder if I would end up feeling a bit disconnected from my workplace.

I don’t think Duet or any other AI agent is quite ready to make us feel like we’re all the CEOs of our own little worlds.

There’s a key word in the title “personal assistant”: personal.

A person can pick up on nuances in tone to understand what’s a big deal and what isn’t.

A person will pick up on communication norms and deploy them sensibly.

A person can be tactful.

Anthropic’s blog post mentions that the company is continuing to “test its judgment about when to message you,” so it’s possible Duet will calibrate a little better over time.

But AI overall isn’t good at understanding nuance or tone, and it’s not clear if it ever will be.

For me, Duet made it a little more clear what I want AI to do for me and what I don’t.

Communication happens all over the place in a modern workplace — in emails, DMs, meetings, shared docs.

Having AI find discrepancies that have been overlooked between all of these sources and point them out proactively is really helpful.

I like it as a backstop for my own organizational systems, not as a replacement for them.

I don’t like it in the creative process.

Like, at all.

I want to find “my own ways into and around a topic,” as Hank Green said of his own reliance on AI .

If you send a robot to do the legwork, you miss the opportunity to stumble across something unexpected.

It’s part of what makes the work enjoyable.

And I’m certainly not about to let an agent review itself for me.

You hear that, Duet?

articles.title: AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI agent & application、Startup & business
articles.summary: LangChain now claims 7,000 customers of its model and platform agnostic agent management tool LangSmith.
articles.full_text:
In Brief Posted: 11:37 AM PST · November 13, 2026 Julie Bort AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday.

That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago , led by IVP.

LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases.

As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents.

It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.

With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs.

It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.

True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well ( case in point is newcomer Mintive ).

However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.
